utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-32-T, the Prosecutor versus Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ossogo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. We are resuming this morning the examination-in-chief of Mr. Amor Masovic, and before we do so, we should like to ask the approval of the Chamber to show about nine minutes of a videotape on some of the sites in question referred to in annexes 1 and 2 of Table B, so as to give you a better insight of the places where these crimes were committed, or rather, where the bodies were buried, and for the Chamber to have a better appreciation of the whole case. And it will be as brief as possible, bearing in mind your observations yesterday to the effect that this examination, including the cross-examination of this witness, should not exceed a certain amount of time. So I hope Your Honours will allow this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I didn't intend to suggest that you were limited to the three hours. I said he had been set down for three hours and we hoped that we would finish within that time. But -- so don't feel that you're bound by any particular time limit, Mr. Ossogo. We'll sit and watch the video if you want us to, and then we'll worry about whether it becomes evidence after we hear Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness comment on the video?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Mr. Amor, please, up to this stage, could you give us some explanations for the site in question and possibly the persons that you were able to recognise who were participating in the exhumation.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So this is a site officially known as Slap 1, which on the map that we had yesterday has been marked as group 2, site 2. In the course of yesterday's testimony, I pointed out that there were 125 victims located at this site who were floating down the Drina in the summer of 1992, and the local population knew that these were civilian non-Serbs, in this particular case exclusively Bosniaks or Bosnian Muslims, who were liquidated in the town of Visegrad and its surroundings. The site that we have seen roughly covers an area which is about 60 metres long, of varying widths, between 8 and 15 metres. The victims were marked with wooden tablets, with ordinal numbers above their heads and legs. In one row there were between at least one and a maximum of eight victims per row. The site is situated about 500 metres from the confluence of the Zepa and the Drina, that is, the point where the Zepa flows into the Drina River. In the latter part of this video, I noticed Mr. Ibrahim Hadzic, who is an investigating judge of the cantonal court in Sarajevo, the district court, and on the video we can also see representatives of my commission, including myself, and the manual workers, who were actually digging up the bodies. In the initial part of the video, one could see Dr. Nermin Sarajlic, who was working on the cleaning of the remains of four victims, using a brush to remove the earth and the sand from the remains. He is a forensic expert attached to the Court in Sarajevo, and he's employed at the Institute for Forensic Medicine of the university in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Masovic. Let us go back to the distinction between civilians or military men among the exhumed bodies. We will continue to view the video now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we stop there for a second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: The two people, Mr. Masovic, could you identify them, please?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't pay sufficient attention. Could you wind back the video for a couple of seconds? Because there are 10 or 15 people there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Does it matter, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and I didn't register who was carrying the bag.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Does it matter? The method being used is of some importance, I suppose, but unless you need to tie it into later evidence, do we really need to know who all these people are?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not of extraordinary importance. Perhaps we can continue. Let us continue with the video, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A brief stop, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, what site is this one where we were able to see numbers up to number 7, I think? Could you tell us which site this is?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is site Slap 2, which is about half a kilometre or a bit more from Slap 1 site, downstream along the Drina, within the Perucac Lake, where there's a canyon and where the lake's banks are rather steep. And one of the witnesses brought us there, or rather, the man who pulled out these seven victims from the waters of the Drina and buried them at that spot. On that occasion, he made a note, or rather, a record, describing the clothing that the victims were wearing at the time of burial, and he also noted that one person was a female and six were males.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The video, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what site this is, Mr. Masovic.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This site is officially known as Jama Paklenik or a pit. It is one of the sites under group 1 on the map and marked with the number 1, so this is a natural cave which is 32 metres deep at first and then, later on, there are several corridors branching off, going as far as 37 metres in depth. A witness brought us to this spot. The witness I will refer to with his initials, SF, who survived an execution that was carried out in the immediate vicinity of this cave and who brought us there, so that from the 15th of August until the 2nd of September last year, we carried out the exhumation of 73 victims from this cave. The identification of these victims showed that our information about this to the effect that they were a group of Bosniak Muslims and a group from Rogatica, so the exhumation confirmed our information. Out of the 73, 65 victims were identified, 44 from the town of Visegrad and 21 from Rogatica. One of the victims, which is typical for this particular site and cave, which we didn't come across in other caves that were processed by my team, one of the victims survived the execution by firearms and only one bullet hit the forearm, his forearm, which was not fatal. This shot was not fatal, and the victim even survived the fall to a depth of 32 metres and, after that, managed to hide in a higher part of the cave that was concealed, and the conclusion of forensic experts is that that victim most probably died of hunger rather than of injuries sustained. In the cave, we identified members of several families, fathers and sons from one family, or rather, from several families fathers and sons, and in one case there were four brothers who were identified by their father.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Masovic, and thank you for the video. We've finished with it. We're now going to go on to the question of identification of these victims. You spoke of a witness whose initials are FS in connection with the victims and bodies discovered at this last site. So let's discuss this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, this is a victim who has already testified before this Chamber, who renounced protective measures, and that is why we can use his name and obtain more details regarding the testimony in connection with this victim. The witness's name is Ferid Spahic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Mr. President. He renounced protective measures and he testified here in open session. We're going to stop there, Mr. Masovic, regarding this site, and we will ask you now to go back to Table B so that we can identify on this table some of the victims on it and that were found in this cave at this site.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Ossogo, that's not yet in evidence. Would it not be better if we made it an exhibit? And also the video, if there is no objection to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. It will be tendered as an exhibit. This was simply for the witness to identify a certain number of names. But if that is not necessary, we can go on, we can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no. My concern is that you keep referring to documents and things, but they're never tendered in evidence. Now, if they're going to be tendered in evidence, they should be. Now, 54/5, I've got a note here, should be tendered. If it has been tendered, I will apologise, but I have no record of it as such. But it was referred to yesterday and explained. You can certainly go to it, but are you going to tender that document? All right. Now, is there any objection to it, Mr. Domazet? Mr. Domazet, is there any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, no objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be Exhibit P54/5. Now, what about the video, before we forget that?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The video, Mr. President, will be 54/6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any objection to that, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be Exhibit P54/6. I've got a note here, whilst we're on the question of exhibits, of 149/1. I'm not sure what it was. I can't find it in the transcript. Certainly 149, which is the map, has gone into evidence. Was there a 149/1? You don't have any reference to it? Well, that's in evidence, so we won't worry at this stage. You proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, could you confirm, listening to the numbers that I am going to tell you, whether they are the persons or victims whose bodies were indeed found at site known as Paklenik, Jama Paklenik, and who are mentioned in annex 1 and 2 of Table B? So I'm going to quote some numbers. The numbers are 54 on Table B, 55, 56, 58.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All these victims were located in the Paklenik cave, and also from numbers 56 through to 59, those are the four brothers, Esad, Hamed, Izet and Mirsad, who were identified in the morgue in Visoko by their father, Ibrahim. 54 and 55 are also two brothers, Sabit and Hasan, the sons of Hamed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: And possibly number 62?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Fikret Karaman.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Kustura Suvad, Kustura Ismet and Kustura Enes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: And 91?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Kustura Medo, son of Meho.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Omerovic Seval and Omerovic Mensur.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kustura Smail, or rather, Smail Omerovic, and Mustafa Omerovic. In some of these cases, these are fathers and sons, or two brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: And 24 and 25, on page 1?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Hilmo and Musan Celik, father and son.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Could you tell us or remind us on the basis of which elements, through testimony of witnesses and other information, were you able to establish that these persons were killed by violent means?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The most important source, which served as a starting point for the identification of these victims, was witness Ferid Spahic, who even before contacting our commission, that is, immediately after surviving the firing squad, after managing to escape from the place of execution, he drew up a list of the people he knew who were in the vehicle together with him on the way to the place of execution. Also, other witnesses knew who were the people in that particular bus which set out from Visegrad, arrived close to the town of Olovo, and then turned back to the area of Sokolac municipality, where the execution was carried out. During the actual identification process of these victims, families played the most important role, because on the basis of clothing, footwear, and personal belongings and documents found on the victims, and coupled with the information that we had obtained from forensic experts who did the autopsy of the victims, they managed to recognise their relatives, with the exception of eight cases, in which the identification has not been completed to this moment in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll stop there for the moment with respect to this site of Paklenik. And I should now like, still referring to Table B, to indicate a few numbers which concern another site. They are victims found in another site, for the purpose of their identification and for telling us possibly about the cause of death. We have number 32, 32, page 1 of Table B, document 54/5; number 33, 34.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were victims who were located on the sites from group 2, in group 2, which is Slap 1, Slap 2, Kamenicko Tocilo and Luke. And they are marked in group 2, marked by the numbers 2, 3, 4 and 5. I'm not sure whether I am able to determine at which of these sites each of these individual victims was found, whether Slap 1 or Slap 2. I think that in the Slap 2 site, where there were seven victims, to the present day none of those persons have been identified. In the Kamenicko Tocilo site, I think that only one person has been identified to date. And on the Luke site, I'm not quite sure how many victims have been identified. The largest number of identified victims from this group, that is to say, group 2, comes from the Slap 1 locality.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's continue. I should like you to look at number 68, 69, and 72, once again Table B, document or Exhibit 54/5.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they were victims who were exhumed on the Slap 1 site: Did you say 75? Did you say number 75?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: No. 72. 72 was the number.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I see. 72, yes. 75 was exhumed from the Paklenik cave, from group 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: And to wind up, I'd like to refer you to number 20 -- 20, 45 - in the same document - 134.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Slap 1 site.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: You said Slap 1 site, did you?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Number 2, on page 1 of Exhibit 54/5. Would you look at that, please.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Agic Emin, Slap 1. Emin Agic, Slap 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Ossogo, I've discovered the missing document that I'm concerned about. It was not 149, it's my bad writing. It's 140/1, which is this map. That's not yet in evidence either. Are you tendering it?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 140. Yes, precisely, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any objection to it, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be Exhibit P140/1. Just keep it in mind, would you, so we don't forget them. Otherwise, we're going to be in trouble at the end; we can't refer to the material we've been looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, for making those observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, you said a moment ago and yesterday -- that is to say, you gave certain indications as to the quality -- as to the state of the bodies of the persons retrieved, and you gave us a partial overview of identification and the process of identification and how you determined civilians and so on. Could you tell us a little more about what and who those persons were. Generally speaking, would you say they were civilians, or were there any army people among them, any soldiers, the bodies that you identified or the bodies that were exhumed but have not been identified as yet. Could you tell us anything more about who the people were?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When speaking about the persons identified, then it is absolutely certain that they were civilians, because this was confirmed by their family members, who identified the bodies, and also there were other indications, that is to say, the clothing they were wearing, the footwear they had, and also the testimony of people who were present during the liquidations, the executions of some of those people who had been identified. That is to say, people who were witnesses when these -- some of these individuals were taken away, taken off. When some of these individuals, some of these victims were arrested and taken into custody and led to certain places where they were detained, there were other people present who witnessed this and saw that, on a certain day, a certain number of victims had been taken away by certain individuals, after which all trace was lost of those persons. Now, talking about the unidentified victims, then it is quite clear that we were able to see, judging from their clothing, that these people were not soldiers, not military men. Otherwise, the commission led by myself, at whose head I am, deals in the quest for missing persons, both civilians and soldiers. But in these particular cases, with the exception of two bodies where they were indeed soldiers, these two were soldiers who had been killed during combat and whose names were written up above their graves. All the other victims, however, were civilians. If necessary, I can identify the two soldiers in question who were buried on a separate site on the Slap 1 site and whose graves have been -- contain their names and surnames, as is customary, according to standard practice, and it is only those two victims who were not brought down by the waters of the Drina but had in fact been killed near the Slap 1 site, and that is why they were buried together with the other civilian victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. You said that, apart from the two soldiers, all the other persons were civilian victims. Now, there were 311 bodies exhumed on the 14 sites, and you indicated this on Table B and its annexes and on the map. You said that they were 311 bodies, minus two means 309 bodies were civilians; is that right? Three hundred and nine bodies were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. civilians?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Actually, the two soldiers did not make up the figure of 311. Three hundred and eleven was the figure of the exhumed civilian victims, whereas the two soldiers are logged in a separate registry book, because they were never categorised as missing persons. And I said in my introduction that we deal with the quest for missing persons, and these two soldiers, their fate was known, both what they did while they were alive and also with regard their date of death. Their parents always knew where they were buried and what had happened to them. And actually, they were exhumed at the request of their families, only because -- only so that after my team had exhumed the remaining 125 victims from that site, only so that those two soldiers should not remain buried alone in that locality once all the other victims had been exhumed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Ossogo, does that mean that the two military men's names or details are not in Exhibit 54/5?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just as the witness has just stated, the names of those two military men are not on that list because they do not make up the number of missing persons who were exhumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Is that right, Witness, they're not on the list?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that, but their name is Galib Seta and Camil Karic and you will not find their names in Table B, which contains 152 names of identified victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: With respect to the identification of civilians, have you any other method of identifying them, apart from clothing and family, their families who identified them? Have you any other means of identification?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in all cases where we suspected that they might be soldiers who were exhumed, when victims of that type were buried, the army of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina becomes involved in the process, and they have their log book in which their members' names are logged. So this is an additional element on the basis of which it is possible to ascertain that in this particular case we are dealing exclusively with civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Based on your experience with these exhumations and everything else that you have gained in the course of your work, could you tell us what the general shape of the body, form of the body was, condition; that is to say, what was the condition of the bodies that were buried? Were there traces of violence on the bodies that you were able to determine and which helped you determine the cause of death, and if so, could you indicate that to the Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to the 311 victims, in each case they were victims who had died in the course of 1992, or, to be more precise, most of these victims were victims who died in the period between April and mid and late August 1992, which means that the bodily remains that we found were skeletal remains exclusively, with elements of clothing, footwear, personal belongings attached to them. Very rarely did we find any personal identification documents. There were no soft tissue -- there was no soft tissue present.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: To go back just for a moment to ethnicity, the ethnicity that the people belonged to, can you give us any indication as to ethnicity, any information in that respect, speaking on those 311 bodies? Can you say anything about ethnicity, which those bodies were?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At present, we can speak exclusively of the national affiliation of the identified victims, the 152 identified victims, and all of them were Bosniak by nationality, or rather, Bosnian Muslims, with the exception of victim under number 101 in Table B, and his name was Adonis Mladenovic, who was from a mixed marriage, that is to say, his parents were of different national affiliation, different ethnicity. Otherwise, let me also say that this victim was from the Rogatica municipality, and that is where the execution took place. It did not take place on the territory of the Visegrad municipality. As for all the other cases, all the other victims, they were all Bosniaks of the Muslim faith, with the exception of persons who were of Albanian origin but they were also of Muslim faith, and they have been marked by the number 114 and 115. Their surname was Nurudini. And also one more number, number 103, and that surname was Mucovski. When speaking about the non-identified victims, I cannot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just a moment, sir. 103, was that an Albanian Muslim or something else?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I've just said that. Yes. He was of Albanian ethnic origin but of the Muslim faith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to the unidentified victims, that is to say, the remaining 159, it is difficult to say with absolute certainty whether they were all Bosniaks, but on the basis of some other pointers, and in certain cases this would be clothing, and in all cases there is the assumption that they were members of the Bosniak population, and this assumption is based on the fact that in the Visegrad municipality area, persons missing are considered persons who became missing in 1992, with a high percentage; that is to say, over 99.9, 99.9 per cent, in fact, is exclusively the Bosniak population. As to the other ethnic groups, we recorded the case of the disappearance of an individual who was a Croat in the Visegrad area. All the other persons, and I'm referring to 1992, were Bosniaks, or rather, Bosnian Muslims. So that is one of the important facts, on the basis of which we are able to assume that the other unidentified victims are also members of the Bosniak nationality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There's still one matter left up in the air, if I may suggest, sir. 101, which you said was of mixed ethnicity, was one of those ethnicities a Bosnian Muslim?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't say with certainty. The father quite certainly was not a Bosnian Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: He was a Serb, by the look of the name, was he?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He would rather -- he would most probably be a Bosnian Croat, as far as I am able to ascertain. The name of the victim is neutral, if I can put it that way, of a neutral character, of Greek denomination, not characteristic for the Balkans, the first name. And the father's name could be both a Bosnian Serb and a Bosnian Croat, but more frequently the name is found amongst Bosnian Croats, actually. As to the victim's mother -- as to the person's mother, and I had contacts with her at least 50 times over the last nine years, because she would come to my office in Sarajevo very frequently searching for her son, I never actually felt the need to determine which ethnicity she was, so that I really can't say for sure whether she is a Bosnian Muslim, a Croat, Serb, or something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, did you have any information in the course of your investigation about the fact that the victims, before being killed, were robbed of their personal effects, their personal property, by illegal means? Was their property confiscated illegally in any way? Do you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not the subject of the work of the commission at whose head I stand. It is our task to search for missing persons. From my personal experience, I can say that I'm aware of the fact that out of almost 11.000 victims which were exhumed by my own team or the Prosecutor's team in the Srebrenica area, in more than 95 per cent of the cases the victims did not have any ID documents on them, personal documents, or any items of value, any valuables. This includes money. We can assume, but that's all we can do, just assume, that their personal documents and money, any items of jewellery and other valuables, had been taken from the victims. But I would not venture to say for sure. I have no knowledge or information about that, nor is that the subject of our expertise. All I can do is note with regret that the confiscation of personal documents, ID documents and personal items, especially pieces of jewellery, makes the process of identification of the victims much more difficult. A ring, a wedding band on a victim's hand can tell you a lot, especially if it has the date of the wedding engraved on it. That could help us enormously in the identification of the victim. Unfortunately, as I have already said, of the almost 11.000 victims that have been exhumed to date, only about 5 per cent of those victims did have any personal documents on them or other items which would help us to identify them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's almost 11.00. I think we had better go back on to the usual timetable. We'll take the adjournment now and resume at 11.30. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Ossogo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. As a preliminary question, I should like to ask for permission to present, through colleague Ms. Bauer, a motion for the protection of a witness. We have just received information about a problem which will take a few minutes. It has to do with the witness who will be examined in-chief tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Bauer.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not quite sure that it is necessary to go in private session. The witness that is called tomorrow, VG115, asked that basically the protective measures are extended to include voice distortion. If the Court needs to hear the reasons for that purpose, I would ask for a short private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We do have to have some reasons, so we'll go into private session for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We are now in public session. Mr. Ossogo, off you go.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Mr. Amor, could you please turn to document 54/1, number 54/1, Table A. Have you found it? This Table A has as attachments two other documents, document 54/2, immediately after the main document, that is, Table 1, and annex 2, which is 54/3 among the OTP documents. Was it you who drew up this document?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I gave instructions to my staff to compile these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Table A is, therefore, a table giving names, and there are 875 names on this table; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: These are persons whose disappearance was noted in the municipality of Visegrad; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: And annex 1 to this table relates to the percentage share in age groups that you attach to this table?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Whereas annex 2 consists of names from the original table listing people who were over 70 years of age?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: In the course of previous testimony in other cases, you indicated the methods that you used to draw up these tables, and you mentioned those methods also when we were talking about the lists of persons exhumed. That is why I will ask you a few questions regarding the procedure used and the comparison between this document and other documents that may come from other sources regarding missing persons in the municipality of Visegrad. Could you please tell us, very briefly, in a few minutes, the process you applied to establish this figure of missing persons in the municipality of Visegrad and in what year did these persons go missing, or what years.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, I wish to say that I am confident that the number of missing persons in the territory of Visegrad municipality is certainly much greater than 875, the number contained in this table for a large number of persons who, in 1991 and the beginning of 1992, were living in Visegrad municipality, disappeared from the territories of some other municipalities during the war, that is, in the period from 1992 to 1995. They may either be neighbouring municipalities, such as Rogatica, Rudo, Cajnice and Gorazde, or they may have gone missing in municipalities which do not border on Visegrad municipality. A number of persons from Visegrad went missing on the mountains while attempting to get out of Visegrad or Gorazde, to which they had originally sought refuge, and it is estimated that about 3.000 Bosniaks from Visegrad fled to Gorazde. A certain number of them attempting to reach Sarajevo or Zenica or Central Bosnia in general, where government forces were in control, went missing. Therefore, this table represents the number of persons who went missing in Visegrad municipality in the course of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there other institutions, local or international, which are engaged in the same kind of work as your commission, that is, in compiling information concerning missing persons and their number?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Local commissions, which are actually departments of our own commission, which is based in Sarajevo, were duty-bound to forward their information and knowledge about the capture or disappearance of persons to our head office in Sarajevo, where that information was systematised. In addition to the local commission, this work was engaged in by certain other state institutions. During the wartime period, they were War Presidencies of the municipalities. Thus, for instance, the War Presidency of Visegrad municipality provided us with this kind of information, and also information about missing persons was forwarded by the police, by military authorities. And in the period after the war, that is, after 1995, an international organisation also set up a database of missing persons in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, and this international organisation is the International Committee of the Red Cross, headquartered in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Are there any differences between the figures that you had and those obtained by the International Red Cross that you mentioned, or did you cooperate amongst yourselves?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is cooperation in complementing databases between those of the local commissions for searching missing persons of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the International Committee of the Red Cross, but there are also discrepancies in the records of missing persons, and as a rule, the local commissions in the territory not only of Bosnia and Herzegovina but also the Republic of Croatia and Yugoslavia and Kosovo, have more complete and voluminous data on missing persons. So the number of missing persons, according to the International Red Cross Committee records with regard to Visegrad municipality, amounts to just over 600, which means that in our records, that is, the records of the commission of which I am the head, there are just over 250 persons whose names are not to be found in the records of the International Red Cross Committee. In my earlier testimony before this Honourable Tribunal, I presented the reasons for these differences, and with your permission, I can repeat them in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just one moment, sir. We'll see whether it's there. Have you checked, Mr. Ossogo, whether that part of it is within the evidence which has been reproduced and tendered? I certainly recall the witness giving the evidence, but I haven't read through this transcript again.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I just thought that he could summarise these reasons regarding Visegrad municipality, because the difference was established in the other case, the case of the Prosecutor versus Milorad Krnojelac with regard to Foca municipality. He could just refer to the principal elements, which explain these differences with regard to Visegrad municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: First of all, I think we have to establish that the material to which the witness has now referred is indeed in the evidence, because the explanation he gave was quite a detailed one and it was very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think it would waste time to ask him to repeat it if it's already here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is document 54/4, Exhibit 54/4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, but what page? Where is the explanation that he gave?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the English version here, not the French one, but it is the testimony given on the 20th of March in 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: He gave evidence in one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Perhaps you could have your case manager look through the transcript and you go on to something else and we can come back to it if it's not in the transcript that we have got here as an exhibit. It is an important issue and it's a very detailed response, and I want to save some time if we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President. We will check through the three days of testimony that the witness gave to find the pages for the relevant explanations, so as not to waste time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, to go back to the document, that is, Table A, concerning persons that have disappeared in this municipality, I should like to refer you to number 397 to 404. It is Exhibit 54/1, 397 to 340 [sic]. This is a series of names, 46 names, which are the same. Perhaps they are families. So could you give us some indication as to what led you to include them in this document of missing persons and any information you have regarding those names.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may, in connection with the previous question, that is, what I said in the other case, and that is that the most important reason for the difference in the records of the International Red Cross and the records that we have is due to the fact that the International Committee accepts applications of disappearance exclusively from immediate family members. Visegrad is an excellent example to identify the difference between the International Committee's records and the records of our commission. In the Foca case, I explained this, and I'm going to repeat it again here. A large number of families, especially --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Please, sir. If we've got it -- we have a lot of your evidence here from the transcript, and if it's in there, you needn't Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. repeat it, because it's already been put into evidence here. It's only if the selection which they have given us here doesn't include that explanation that we'll come back and ask you for it. So you had perhaps better answer the question that was asked of you in relation to the various numbers in document numbered 54/1. You've called it an exhibit, Mr. Ossogo, but it is not an exhibit; it hasn't been tendered yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. We are going to tender it in a moment. It is document 54/1 of the Office of the Prosecutor, which indeed is still not an exhibit but which we are going to tender after using it during this examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: So let me repeat my question. So I'm referring to the names starting from 397 to 440, which are to be found in this document and which are the same names.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite right. This is the (redacted), which originally came from Koritnik, or rather, most of them were living in the area of Koritnik village in Visegrad municipality. And I think that our records contain 46 names of members of the (redacted) who at this point in time are considered missing persons. In the records of the International Committee for the Red Cross, I think that not more than 12 to 15 have been recorded, and that is what I wanted to draw attention to in my response a moment ago. A very small number of the (redacted) members survived the year 1992 in Koritnik, or in Visegrad, and simply very few members of their immediate family remain who could submit a search request to the International Red Cross Committee. We have here a large number of close relatives, parents and children, brothers, brothers and sisters, closest family members, uncles, aunts. In some cases there are three generations: Grandfathers, parents, and children -- grandparents, parents, and children. Unfortunately, the (redacted) is not the only one to be represented in such a large number among the missing persons. If you look at other parts of this same list, you will find, on page 1 of this document, the Ahmet Spahijic family, of whom 14 are missing. On page 2 of the document, the Avdic family, of whom, again, 14 are missing. On page 3 of the document, the Besirevic family, of whom 9 are missing. And if you go through the list to the end, you will find that there are cases when in some families more than 20 persons are still missing and nothing is known about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: According to the principle that you have just told us about, these are indeed family members who contacted you, specifically regarding the [redacted].

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: I should also like to refer you to number 87 and 90 of this same document; 54/1, 87 and 90. I'm just referring to the numbers, because these are names again of persons, protected persons in these proceedings. Do you know by whom you were informed before putting these names on the list of missing persons? I am talking about numbers 87 and 90.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you each first and last name from this list, but it was mostly family members who informed us about their immediate relatives who went missing. Just now I really am unable to answer the question how this family, [redacted], or the eight members of that family were included in this list. I assume that one of their relatives came to our department in Gorazde, or to the head office in Sarajevo, and reported that they are missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: After having identified the bodies and having registered them in your files, did you separate the bodies that you identified and those that were not identified? So did you delete them from this list of missing persons once you found their bodies?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were deleted from the list of missing persons, but they were kept in our records, with the note that the victims had been located, exhumed, and identified and buried. But they are no longer kept in the record of missing persons and their names are not found in this document. They are in a separate document consisting of 152 identified persons, and this document is also here in this file as Table B.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, to go back to the transcript, page -- I'm not sure of the page. No. It is page 5267 -- 4267 of Exhibit 54/4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's the bald statement, yes. I thought that the witness had given a lot more detail. Sir, you are recorded in the previous trial as having said of the Red Cross, or the International Committee of the Red Cross this: "Their information is scantier because they record missing persons. Only family members have reported them as such, whereas we have broader criteria and I already explained at the beginning of my testimony who are all the persons and organisations that can submit information to us in order to register persons as missing." Now, my recollection is that at some other stage in the course of your evidence you gave a more detailed explanation. It may be that it will be quicker if we take it from you again than to try and find it. If you want to add to that explanation, please do.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. With the exception of the family members, we accepted all notification for other individuals whom we knew or assumed could have any knowledge as to the disappearance of certain persons. For example, witnesses who were present when one person or a group of persons were taken away are a very valuable source of information on the disappearance of certain individuals, and in cases like that, the family members did not have any direct knowledge of the disappearance of their relatives but there are witnesses who saw them being taken off, individual or a group. Sometimes those groups numbered several tens of persons whom the witness knew and recorded. He would register the date and time the people were taken away and, afterwards, these people were never seen or heard of again. So in addition to that type of witness, we have former prisoners or former inmates who registered the presence of their inmates in certain camps and prisons and those detainees were taken out of the prison or camp where they were held and never appeared again. In the case of Foca, as in the case of Visegrad, there are a certain number of witnesses who were prisoners at one time, former inmates, who during the war were exchanged with the help of commissions, and I worked with these commissions. And those victims testified that a certain number of men from Visegrad prisons such as the Uzamnica prison were taken out, never to be returned to the prison again. Apart from these direct sources of knowledge concerning missing persons, we also received information of this kind from the information that the local police organs and military organs came by, as well as the wartime presidencies, and as I said in the course of my testimony yesterday, from the database which the International Red Cross Committee has at its disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there anything you want to ask further, Mr. Ossogo?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. At this stage, Mr. President, we would like to tender documents 54/1 and the annex, which annex is marked 54/2 and 54/3, annexes 1 and 2, as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. They will be Exhibits P54/1, 54/2, and 54/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that completes our examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Masovic, Exhibit 141, the map titled the Exhumations Conducted in Visegrad Municipality, my question is the following: According to your commission and its findings, were they victims from the territory of Visegrad municipality or does this just show the exhumation sites on the territory of that municipality?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The title of the document is somewhat different. The heading is different. In the Bosnian language it would be translated as "Exhumation in Connection to the Visegrad Municipality," so not exhumation on the territory of Visegrad. And from the document it is clearly evident that these 14 sites or localities were not all on the territory of Visegrad municipality. The number 1 group is in the Sokolac municipality, for example. But during my testimony I explained that it was the case of a bus with prisoners coming from Visegrad, originating from Visegrad, and in that bus Mr. FS was in the bus too. The bus was sent towards Olovo and then sent back to the Kalimanici locality, or rather, the Paklenik mountain, where these 50-odd victims were liquidated and thrown into a 32-metre-deep pit or cave. The locality, or rather, group 2, the next site, partially encompasses - and we're talking about Slap 1 and Slap 2 here, sites 2 and 3 - lie in the locality of the Rogatica municipality, and it is the yellow shaded area on the map, but the victims floated down the Drina River from the town of Visegrad and its surroundings. Group 3, all the sites are on the Visegrad territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Part of my question referred to that, because it says on the map that there were 14 places and 311 bodies in total that were exhumed. From what you have just explained, a portion of those, and you know the exact number, in the Rogatica municipality does not refer to these victims and the events in Visegrad. That is certain, is it not?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In group number 1 at least 21 victims originate from the Rogatica municipality, and they were executed in the town of Rogatica and brought dead to the area above the Paklenik cave and thrown into that same cave where the victims from Visegrad were executed and thrown into. So there we're dealing with 21 individuals from the Rogatica area, and that has been clearly designated in Table B, which contains 152 names of identified victims, and they originate from the Rogatica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You have just mentioned the table containing all these facts and data. I didn't notice, and I don't think it is included in the tables, because there were some questions from Mr. Ossogo on that matter as well. What I'm talking about is different persons under different numbers, and you were telling us where the bodies were found. Now, my question is as follows: Why did you not compile a table which would show where the bodies of the identified persons were exhumed? Because that would facilitate your investigation considerably.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid that a table like that could lead to some confusion if we were to separate the bodies belonging to Visegrad. Then we would have to include all the previous exhumations that we conducted in the Rogatica area, and I think that there were more than 400 victims exhumed to date from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I don't think you understood me. My question was the following: Let us take an example, 54, 55, and 56, those numbers. Mr. Ossogo asked you where those individuals were exhumed and you said, I think, Paklenik. Now, my question is: Why is that piece of information not included in the table? Because that would facilitate checking out the Slap 1 or other areas marked by you.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you there. If what is important for you is to know where each of the victims were exhumed, from which grave site, if you need to know that, I would be happy to answer your questions. I can tell you where each of these 152 victims were exhumed, in which mass grave or individual grave. If that is essential and vital for you, I can answer that question for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. What I was asking you was merely whether this exists as a separate piece of information, and you said no. Yes, you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Does that mean, Mr. Domazet, that you do not want that information; it's just a criticism of the method, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, I would have preferred to have had that information, because then I could go through those persons to see if any of them have anything to do with this trial. But I'm not going to ask the witness what Mr. Ossogo did, because he asked him specifically about some individuals who could be connected to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But the witness has offered to give you that information. I'm not suggesting we go through each of the 152 at this stage, but if, before he leaves, he marked up a copy of this particular table with the particular exhumation site, if you want it, we'll ask him to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, sir, perhaps, if you could before you leave, go through the table and insert the particular site, exhumation site for each of the 152. You said you were able to do it. Now, would you do it -- when you finish giving your evidence, would you be able to do it for us on a copy of one of these exhibits?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That will take me 15 minutes, and I can do that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. We look forward to it. You proceed, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, in answering questions about identification, ethnicity, the ethnicity of the victims, you said that most of them, or practically all of them, belonged to the Bosniak Muslim category. You used a term and said that they were all of Muslim faith and that that was one of the criteria. Do you not think that that need not be the case because they might have been atheists and that there were many of those in our former country. There were quite a lot of atheists. I assume that you thought that most of them were what you said they were by virtue of faith, but did you think about the atheists?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were objective reasons why I said that. When a victim is identified, we move to its burial, and on the basis of the ceremony, the funeral, the burial ceremony itself and the traditions applied there, it is very easy to see which faith the victim belonged to. Let me tell you that on the 5th of August, for example, this year, in Visegrad more than 150 identified and unidentified victims were buried. They had their funerals there. And those funerals were held in keeping with Islamic customs and tradition. So this is indicative and an objective way of concluding that the victims were indeed of the Muslim -- of the Islamic faith. I can agree with you that affiliation to the Bosniak nation need not, at the same time, mean belonging to the Islamic faith, but I know of no example in the Visegrad case which would indicate that the people were not members of the Islamic faith at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Masovic. You have explained one criterion for us which is a possible one, that is to say, the funeral, which can indicate ethnicity and faith. Although we're dealing with just one case and therefore it's particularly not too important, I would like to refer for a minute to victim 101, whom you said was from a mixed marriage in which the father was a Bosnian Croat or Bosnian Serb, so that criterion there was not checked out in the way you have just described to us for you to be able to give us your opinion. So although you said that the name Tihomir can be both a Croatian and Serbian name, and I agree with that, but Mladenovic is more typically a Serbian name, and I'm sure you'll agree with that.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely so. The mother of this victim, as I said, contacted me about 50 times over the past eight or nine years, and I know that this victim was buried in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said, Mr. Masovic, that only about 5 per cent of those victims, the exhumed victims, had on them any documents or items which could identify them. Does that mean that all the other ones who were identified were identified on the basis of witnesses or family member testimony or in similar ways by people being able to recognise the bodies on the basis of some factors?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In most cases we relied on the testimony of the victims' immediate families, if they survived. If not, then on the basis of the broader family members or witnesses who had knowledge of what the victim looked like, what they were wearing the day they disappeared, and of course, on the basis of anthropological characteristics of the victim, that is to say, the height of the victim, the teeth, any possible fractures which the victims had suffered in the course of their life and which were common knowledge to their relatives. And quite recently, but we can't speak of this as a general method, the identification of victims at least in the Srebrenica case is being conducted with the help of DNA analyses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. That was what I was interested in, looking at Visegrad, because if we're talking about the identification of exhumed persons who were exhumed mostly in the year 2000, eight years later, and as you yourself said, they were skeletons mostly, I assume that identification on the basis of recognition by relatives is a very rare occurrence, relatives or friends, after so much time with the skeletons you had.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On the contrary, I said that the most common way of identification was with the help of the family members. But you must be aware of one particular fact, and that is that in the Paklenik cave, for example, we had 73 victims. Of that number, we knew that 50 of them were in the bus with the witness who survived the execution, and that witness I think knew 47 names of the victims who were in the bus with him. That means that we were able to narrow down the potential circle of victims from 875, which was the total number that had disappeared on the overall territory of Visegrad municipality, and the victims from the Paklenik cave was narrowed down to 50 persons, those 50 who the witness had seen when they were executed, he was present. It was our task, of those 50, to determine who was Esad, who was Mirsad, who was Enes, for example, who was Adonis, and so on and so forth. So our task wasn't an overly difficult one with respect to identification. In some other cases, such as Slap 1, for example, I've already said that the people pulling out the bodies from the River Drina took out fresh bodies, so to speak, who were recognisable at first glance because they had been killed one or two days before, upstream, upstream from Slap in Visegrad, and refugees from Visegrad who worked on the retrieval of these bodies, pulling them out, were able to ascertain the identity of the victims on the spot, so that that fact made our identification task much more easy. The skeletons, we found eight years after the event had taken place. Our task was facilitated in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Masovic. I understand you. The situation is quite different when the bodies were pulled out one or two days after death or ten days after death, and there were cases like that. I know that. So that that is quite certainly easier. But my question focused on the bodies this wasn't done: In Slap 1, eight years later, was it possible to identify the bodies on the basis of what the relatives said or was this only possible on the basis of forensic experts? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both. Both the anthropological characteristics of the victim and what the witnesses and family members said. Putting those two together, we were able to identify the victims. Unfortunately, from the documents that you have before you, it is evident that even more than 50 per cent of the victims to the present day have not been identified, which means that either no family members remain or witnesses who were able to help us out in the identification process or, quite simply, the condition of the skeleton, of the victim, was such that it was impossible to make any form of classical identification. It is only with the help and application of DNA analysis, on condition that some family members are living and specific family members, because the DNA analysis requires that we look at the descendents on the female side, female antecedents and then compare the DNA structure of the blood of live relatives with the DNA structure of the bones of the victim. Only by applying that method will it maybe be possible over the next five or seven years, it might may be possible to establish the identity of the remaining 159 Visegrad victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I understand fully what you're saying, Mr. Masovic. Among the identified persons, as they were identified in various stages and in various ways, as you have just explained, do you consider this to be completely reliable or is it possible to consider that there may have been some errors, more or less of them?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's really not a single reason of an objective or a subjective nature that would lead me to think that these 152 victims are not precisely the persons indicated by their family members. So if you want a straightforward answer, I'm absolutely confident that no error was made in the process of their identification, that the family members recognised them with the help of elements provided by the forensic experts and that they really recognised their family members and identified them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: There were cases, Mr. Masovic, that people who were burying those bodies in Slap 1, that they recognised some of those bodies and they marked the graves. Was their statement sufficient for you, or did you check those statements out through family members and medical experts as well?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course we did not rely only on identification by laymen. The establishment of the identity of the bodies, in accordance with the laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina, has to be established by a commission consisting of the investigating judge, the Prosecutor, a crime technician or a policeman, and a forensic medical expert; and even in the case I mentioned in the introductory part of my testimony, even in the case of those two members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, of whom we knew with certainty that they were precisely those persons, as they were buried by their relatives, who marked their graves with their first and last name - Seta Galib, Karic Camil - even in that case, we checked out their identity, and I even had to answer a question put by Galib Seta's father, who asked me, "Why are you doing this? Why is further verification of identity required when he as the father knows with certainty that that is his son, that he was buried there in Slap?" And my answer simply was that this was a legal requirement which we have to observe, regardless of whether the parents wish it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you mentioned these two soldiers who were separated and you explained this to us, the question of their uniforms, this brings me to my next question: Would it be possible among these victims wearing civilian clothes, that there may have been persons who may have taken part in the war operations and lost their life in those operations in view of the time period in question and when, according to abundant evidence, many belonged to various formations without having any military uniforms, which could be a very important identifying factor. So could it be possible that even among these who have been identified as civilians to have been killed as a soldier on any of the sides, warring sides?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very difficult to make such an assumption. Why? The vast majority of those 125 bodies arrived in the period from the beginning of June up to mid-August or the end of August 1992. If you are familiar with the military situation in Visegrad at the time, then it is quite clear that this area upstream of Slap, in the direction of Visegrad, was under the control of the Serb army, so that there were in fact no military operations there. If we were dealing with some other areas where there were occasional clashes between the armies, then there would be grounds to assume that among the victims there may have been people who were killed in battle. In this case, it is indeed difficult to assume that any one of the victims could have been a victim of a direct confrontation of two warring armies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. Masovic, but according to the testimony of some witnesses in this case, in these proceedings, we were told that from June, sometime around the 10th of June, if I'm not mistaken, they belonged to the Muslim, not Serb brigade, which in those villages along the Drina were active, and that is where they were positioned immediately after leaving the territory conditionally speaking under Serb control. They explained that they became members of such-and-such a brigade. I assume that they didn't have uniforms, and we have some evidence and photographs confirming this. Now, whether they could have got killed in operations, that's another matter, but there is evidence that such military formations did exist in the territory of Visegrad from the month of June onwards. But of course that is not part of your testimony or your expertise. But my next question, as you're focusing on Visegrad, is: Is it possible for these corpses to have come along the Drina but from places further removed from Foca or Gorazde, that those corpses may have come from one of these locations and been buried in Slap 1 or Slap 2?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are at least two reasons due to which my answer to your question is no. The first reason is that among the 125 identified victims, or rather, 52 persons identified from Slap, 125 exhumed, there's not a single one who went missing in any other area outside of the town of Visegrad. Therefore, all those who were identified went missing in Visegrad. Regarding the non-identified persons, we cannot tell where they disappeared from, because we don't know their identity, but we do know that in the town of Visegrad, upstream from the town itself, there is a hydro power station. There's an artificial dam on the Drina River which would prevent the flow of any material, and therefore including bodies passing through that dam. So it is quite clear that all the victims were liquidated downstream from the Visegrad power plant dam, and unfortunately, we can by now state that those two dams of the Visegrad hydro power station and the other one in Bajna Basta, that is, the Perucac hydro power station dam have probably forever destroyed a very large number of victims from the territory of Visegrad and downstream from Visegrad, and from Foca, which is upstream from Visegrad. The bodies reached the turbines of the power plant and probably there's nothing left of those bodies. So I'm absolutely certain, to come back to your question, that all the victims to be found in graves Slap 1, Slap 2, Kamenicko Tocilo and Luke marked in group 2 as sites 2, 3, 4, and 5, come from the area of Visegrad municipality or the town of Visegrad itself. There are another three sites, at least, of which we are sure, and they are downstream from Visegrad, that they contain dozens of new bodies of victims from Visegrad, but we have still not managed to exhume those victims because we are collecting data which could be helpful in identifying those victims, and we will probably, at the beginning of next year, start on those exhumations as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, I understand the two reasons that you have given. Allow me, with regard to this second, regarding the dam, I do know that there is the dam on the hydro power station, and clearly if a body reaches the turbines, no traces would be left of them. But we are also aware that the water was released from the dam in large quantities for some similar reasons. So I personally believe - I don't know whether you will agree - that in those cases, when the water was released from the dam, bodies could have come from upstream. I would agree with you that this may apply to a smaller number, that the majority come from this area, but I really don't think you could exclude that possibility. But I'm asking you just once more. I won't dwell on it any further.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am really not an expert for such matters. You would have to call someone working on hydro power plants to give an explanation. All I can do is repeat what I have said, and that is: Out of the 52 identified victims in site Slap 1, absolutely each and every one of them was from Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, didn't one of the witnesses tell us the date upon which the first body came down? That was well after the water had been released, and you didn't challenge that date. It's an interesting theory, but it seems, if I may say so, not to be in accordance with the evidence we've got. There may be some other evidence coming in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wasn't referring to that particular release that witnesses spoke of. That is true, that happened much earlier. It was a few days prior to the arrival of the Uzice Corps, if I'm not mistaken, and then at least there were no killings, at least no large-scale killings. That was when the water was released and flooding occurred of some settlements, but that's something else. I'm referring to the situation when water was released over the dams, not into the turbines, over the dams for various reasons, and as I have seen, it is being alleged that some persons intentionally released the water to raise the water level for the bodies to flow down the Drina. So I'm talking about those occasions. But of course, that is a matter that needs to be proven, and of course the witness is not an expert, nor am I, for that particular situation. As regards the first reason that you have given, which is a logical one, but don't you think that it would be very difficult to expect families of missing persons further upstream, that is, Gorazde and Foca, could take part in procedures taking place close to Visegrad, so it is normal that relatives and friends living close by could be there; if there were any cases of bodies coming further upstream, that it would be unlikely for their family members to be present?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All family members were given an opportunity to attend, so the invitation was addressed to all persons who were searching for their dear ones. It is true that families mostly focus on their area, but there are family members who have been coming to attend all identification procedures for three or four years, wherever they may be in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So I cannot give you a specific answer whether this particular identification process was attended by anyone from Foca or Gorazde. I can't answer that question. But everyone could attend each of the identification procedures, and I can tell you that we in the commission are doing everything in our power to have as many families respond to these calls, because the success of our work is measured not only by the number of exhumed victims but particularly by the number of identified victims. So that it is very important for us for as many victims to be identified as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I quite understand that the purpose of your commission is to have as many bodies identified as possible and to have the largest possible percentage share of identified victims. That is why I asked you this question about reliability, because I expressed the fear that in some cases there may have been mistakes. But you have told us that that -- you think that was not possible. A question has to do with your terminology. I don't know whether it was a slip of the tongue or not. You used the term "mass grave." In my view, and on the basis of what I have read, a mass grave has to consist of a large number of bodies. In this case, Paklenik could be described in this way. But according to the evidence we have, these were bodies that were mostly buried one next to another, so I don't think we can use the term "mass grave." Maybe you used it because you felt that a large number of people were buried in the area.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am really not sure, because in the world there are different theories as to what can be defined as a mass grave. Some prominent forensic experts that I have worked with of worldwide renown, such as Mr. William Haglund, from the United States of America, consider a mass grave it be a grave in which three or more victims are buried. At the local level in Bosnia-Herzegovina, we consider a mass grave to be one in which five or more persons are buried in one grave. So there are two different criteria: It has to be one grave, a single grave, and to contain at least five victims. I have explained that Slap 1 covers an area that is about 60 metres long and between 8 and 15 metres wide, that the graves are lined up in file. In some rows there is only a single grave and in other lines there are up to eight graves. There are places with four or five victims inside, and you were able to see this on the video when there are four or five victims buried in the same grave, which means that a single grave was dug, 2 by 2 metres in size, into which four or five victims were laid. And that is why I used the term "mass grave," but I could agree with you that this was not the mass grave in the strict sense of the word, in which victims were thrown in one on top of another without any order, and such graves, in my personal experience, there were more than 200 such graves in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In this case, it is quite evident what we are dealing with. As the local Bosniak population was burying the victims, they did so as much as they could in a civilised and decent manner, so that there was some order to it, putting the victims one next to another rather than throwing them one on top of another, as we found in group 1 in the Paklenik site or in some other cases, at the Kurtalici site, for instance, where 62 victims were located, some seven or eight kilometres downstream from Visegrad on the right bank of the Drina River, where the victims were completely mixed together and where it is virtually impossible to separate which part of the skeleton belongs to which victim. And that is why very few of the victims at this site were identified. Only six out of 62 have been identified on this site, precisely because of the way in which the victims were buried, if they were buried at all, because this was an area which most of the year is below the level of the water in the lake, and only when the season is extremely dry and the water level is exceptionally low, the water level in the lake, is it possible to reach that site and discover this mass grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic talking about Paklenik - I think that is the name - which is certainly a mass grave, as you explained, you have a very large percentage of identified victims, and you explained to us that witness SF, he is not a protected witness, therefore I can name him, Ferid Spahic, that he gave you the names of 47 persons, if I'm not mistaken, that he said were killed there. As I see, 44 were identified. So my question is: Was it on the basis of his statement or was the identity of each of these bodies verified to make sure who they were, so that only in a few number of cases were you unable to establish the identity?

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In each of the cases, the identity was established individually. There are at least another four names, I think, that is, the victims we know of. We know their first and last names, we know that they are in the Paklenik cave. But their families, on the basis of what we found there, were unable to confirm their identity. They were buried as "NN," that is, non-identified, name unknown, and samples of bone were taken from remains of skeletons and DNK [as interpreted] analysis is underway in the US to establish the identity of the remaining victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Masovic, another point in connection with ethnicity. When you said that you believe that all or almost all of them were Bosniak Muslims or Bosniaks, and you said that 99.9 per cent of the missing persons were Bosniaks, that only one Croat has been reported missing. So my question is: In view of the commission and the division between ethnic groups at the time, did the Serbs at all report any disappearances to you? As far as I know, no missing Serb would be -- the disappearance of a Serb would not be reported to your commission, as far as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of the war, from 1992 to 1995, indeed a very small number of persons of the Bosnian Serb population would report the disappearance of their relatives to our commission in Sarajevo.
