In the post-war period, and especially during the last two years, there are more and more Bosnian Serbs who are coming and reporting the disappearance of their loved ones to our commission in Sarajevo. Probably - I hope this will not sound immodest on my part - probably also because of the 11.000 victims that we have managed to exhume in the last five years alone or with the help of investigators from the Tribunal. However, persons of all ethnicities were able to report not only to local commissions but also to the International Committee of the Red Cross. So if you look at the records of the International Committee of the Red Cross relevant to the town of Visegrad, out of more than 600 reported disappearances, only one Bosnian Serb has been registered, and he disappeared in April 1993. His name is Stevan Pesic and he disappeared somewhere around Medzedza in Visegrad municipality. I said earlier on that a Bosnian Croat had been reported missing. His surname is Loncaric, who disappeared in the town of Visegrad, simultaneously with the Bosniaks from that town. So those are the data of the International Committee of the Red Cross, which could be considered a completely neutral organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. [In English] My last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Actually, maybe I wouldn't be asking this question at all, but this answer of yours I think differs significantly from what we were given as written testimony by Witness Eva Tabeau and a diagram showing that among the missing persons there were a large number of Serbs, many more than the number you have given in 1992, but we have that report too, and these were reports from the International Red Cross. But that is probably not too important. Thank you anyway. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: AMOR MASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do have that document of the International Committee of the Red Cross, which is called Missing Persons on the Territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it can be seen from this document on page 355 that Pesic Stevan disappeared in Medzedza on the 12th of April, 1993. If you mean that there were other Serbs among the 600 or so, then will you please help me find them? I was unable to find any missing Serbs in this document, apart from this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sir, during the luncheon adjournment, would you take a copy of annex B and note on it from which exhumation site each of the 152 victims was taken. I hope it won't take up too much time of your lunch break. I should have recorded in the transcript that in Exhibit 54/4, which is the transcript of Mr. Masovic's evidence in the Krnojelac case, there's also a reference to the difference between his figures and the ICRC figures at pages 4348 to 4351. We'll come back at 2.30 for the re-examination, if any. Thank you. We'll adjourn now. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.01 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, has this document been completed that we requested? It has indeed. Well, Mr. Domazet, except for the heading of Mass Grave Site, is there any problem you have with this document? It seems to be the answer to what you had sought.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well, then. Mr. Ossogo, what do you suggest we call it? 54/7?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You need your microphone on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's it, I think, Mr. President, but let me just make sure. Yes, Mr. President, it is 54/7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be Exhibit P54/7. Thank you, sir, very much for having compiled that for us. It will be of assistance to us, and we're grateful to you for the time you took. Now, any re-examination, Mr. Ossogo?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, thank you again for coming to give evidence here. We'll probably be seeing you from case to case in relation to these problems. We're grateful to you for coming here and for the time you spent in preparing the matter for us. You are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, we're starting with VG115 tomorrow. Is there any realistic estimate of how long that witness will take?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my colleague will be conducting that examination, but we expect it to last a little less than two morning sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Why I ask is that we have got a fairly tight schedule with the witnesses on the videolink, and that if we don't finish them, I'm not sure whether we've got the videolink available to us on Friday as well. It's all right. I'm told that the videolink will be available on the Friday. So that's all right. I was concerned that we should give priority to the videolink witnesses, but if that's the way we have to deal with it, then we'll deal with 115 first thing in the morning. Very well. Is there anything else that we need or can -- need to or can dispose of now?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President, no other problems to submit to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: How about you, Mr. Domazet? Have you got anything else you want to raise at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, Your Honour; for the moment, nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Very well. We'll adjourn now and resume at 9.30 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 26th day of September, 2001, at 9.30 a.m. 25
